prime.problem: The model's layers end in raw scores that can be negative or huge. You can't average with them or sample a word from them until they're positive and add to 1, and the obvious fix (divide by the sum) gives negative "probabilities".
prime.fits: First stop that turns vectors into weights. It takes the rows of numbers that the embedding and matrix-multiply cards produce, and it's used twice: on attention scores (next card) and on the logits at the top (the loss card).
expect: exp, then divide by the row's total
prime.goal: Compute a softmax row by hand with the max trick, explain why exp is used, and predict what temperature and masking do to the shares.

attend: Dividing the logits by their sum also makes them add to 1. What exactly goes wrong with it on the tiny model's last row?
Why does subtracting the row's largest score leave every share unchanged, and what does it prevent?
Why does mat's share relate only to the gap between its score and the others, not to the scores' size?
If temperature can sharpen or flatten the shares, why can it never change which word is on top?
How does a score of −inf let attention ignore future tokens without removing them from the row?

must: exp of any number is positive and grows with its input → every share is above 0 and the order of the scores is kept → dividing by the total makes the row add to 1 (last logits row: total 15.2629, mat \(11.3000 / 15.2629 = 0.7404\))

\(\exp(a) \div \exp(b) = \exp(a - b)\) → only the gaps between scores matter → subtracting any constant \(c\) from the whole row cancels as \(e^{-c}\) on the top and bottom → subtracting the max gives the same p, and the largest exp becomes exactly 1
float32 \(\exp\) overflows above 88.72 → \(\exp(1000)\) = inf and inf ÷ inf = nan → shifting \([1000,\ 999,\ 998]\) to \([0,\ -1,\ -2]\) gives \([0.6652,\ 0.2447,\ 0.0900]\) safely

Dividing by \(T > 0\) scales every gap by the same factor and keeps the order → small \(T\) widens the gaps (mat 0.9652 at \(T = 0.5\)), big \(T\) narrows them (0.4628 at \(T = 2\)) → a sampling dial that can't change the top word
elevated: \(\exp(-\infty) = 0\) exactly → a masked score contributes nothing to the top or bottom of the fraction → the causal mask is just −inf written into the score grid before softmax
The max trick prevents overflow but not underflow → with very large logits the right word's \(p\) rounds to 0 and \(-\log p\) is inf → real code computes log-softmax in one step
reference: Softmax always runs along the last axis, one row at a time: exp(z) / exp(z).sum(-1, keepdims=True)
\(\exp\) overflow ceilings: float32 and bfloat16 88.72, float16 11.09
PyTorch: torch.softmax(x, dim=-1) does the max subtraction internally

compress.prompt: From memory, write the softmax formula and explain in 3–4 sentences why it uses exp, why code subtracts the max first, and what temperature does. Or redraw the five-bar sketch: scores → exp → ÷ total → shares.
checklist: exp makes every score positive and keeps their order; dividing by the total makes the row add to 1
dividing raw scores by their sum gives negative values and values above 1
only gaps matter, so a shift by the max cancels; it stops exp from overflowing (above 88.72 in float32)
temperature divides the scores by \(T\): small \(T\) sharpens, big \(T\) flattens, the order never changes
\(-\infty\) gives exactly 0, which is how masking works; softmax is used for attention weights and for next-token probabilities

retrieve.q: Explain why softmax exponentiates the scores instead of dividing them by their sum, using what goes wrong on the tiny model's last logits row.
answer: the scores sum to 2.0667 and \(z / \operatorname{sum}(z)\) gives \(-0.2591\) and \(1.1732\): below 0 and above 1
a row summing to 0 would divide by zero
\(\exp\) is always positive, keeps the order, and turns gaps into ratios

retrieve.q: Walk through computing softmax of \([0.4570,\ 2.0006,\ -2.1253]\) the way tiny.py does it, naming each intermediate.
answer: total 1.2298

retrieve.q: Your model is generating repetitive, safe text. Would you raise or lower the temperature, what do you gain, and what do you risk?
answer: raise \(T\): the gaps shrink, so lower-ranked words get more share and get sampled more
gain: variety
risk: more nonsense, because unlikely words get picked more often; at \(T = 2\) mat drops from 0.7404 to 0.4628
\(T\) only reshapes the shares; it can't make a better word the top one

retrieve.q: Removing the max-subtraction line from tiny.py changed nothing. Argue whether it's safe to drop it from a real model's code.
answer: tiny's largest logit is 2.4248, far under the 88.72 ceiling, so nothing overflowed
real models can produce larger scores, and float16 overflows above just 11.09
with \(\Wout \times 1000\) the copy without it gave nan; the subtraction costs one pass over the row
keep it: it's nearly free and changes no answer

compare.q: Softmax sits right after \(QK^\top/\sqrt{d}\). Dividing by \(\sqrt{d}\) and dividing by a temperature \(T\) are both a division before softmax. What does each one fix, and when is each chosen?
answer: \(\sqrt{d}\) is fixed by the head size and keeps scores from growing with \(d\), so attention doesn't saturate during training
\(T\) is chosen at generation time to make sampling sharper or flatter
both rescale the gaps, so both keep the order
\(\sqrt{d}\) is part of the model; \(T\) is not used in training

compare.q: The loss takes −log of one softmax output. Why do \(\exp\) (in softmax) and \(\log\) (in the loss) pair so well, and what numerical problem does computing them separately cause?
answer: \(\log\) undoes \(\exp\), so \(-\log p = -z_{\tgt} + \log \sum_j \exp(z_j)\): no division left
separately, a tiny \(p\) can round to 0 and \(-\log\) gives inf
so real code uses log-softmax / cross-entropy in one step, with the same max subtraction inside

compare.q: Karpathy's bigram model also exponentiates and normalises, but its scores come from one table lookup. What is the same, and what does a transformer change about where the scores come from?
answer: same function: exp, then divide by the row's total
bigram: a row of the table is the score row, picked by the previous character
transformer: the score row is computed from the whole context through attention and the FFN
the softmax step itself doesn't care where the scores came from

predict.q: Attention row 1 has one real score and two −inf cells. Suppose instead that every cell in a row were −inf (a token allowed to see nothing). What would softmax return, and why?
predict.answer: nan for every entry. Every \(\exp\) is 0, so the total is 0, and \(0 \div 0\) is undefined. Even the max trick can't help, because the max is \(-\infty\) and \(-\infty - (-\infty)\) is nan. That's why the causal mask always leaves the diagonal open: each token can at least see itself.
